“Yes, so have I,” said Constance. “I wish he would marry a rich lady.”

“Shall we put our heads together and see if we can find him one?” Lorck asked with a smile.

Constance laughed.

“When we get home, we shall be really pleasant to him, Constance. I think he likes being with us.”

“Yes, really pleasant,” Constance replied.

“Besides, he was surely madly smitten with you for a while, you know. Didn’t you notice anything?”

“Not a trace,” was the answer.

“Did he never hint at any such thing?”

“Never!” Constance replied.

“No, he is a refined and well-bred person,” Lorck thought, and offered a quiet sigh to the memory of his own conduct.

“Besides, it has probably only been a quite passing fit that he had,” he said aloud.

“Did he say anything to you about it, then?” Constance asked with a half-roguish, half-wondering smile.

“No indeed, not one blessed whit,” Lorck assured her. “It may well be that it was merely a fancy of mine; I went around thinking that everyone must fall in love with you, you see.”

They both remained silent for a few minutes.

“What are you thinking about, my Conny?” Lorck then said, reaching for her hand.

“Nothing, really,” she said kindly.

“Nonsense, tell me now,” he begged, drawing her closer to him.

“Well, that is easier said than done. Sometimes one’s thoughts run so wild, or they come in little fragments and are so disconnected, or it is sheer foolishness that one sits there being driven around by; it is quite impossible to find words for it.”

He had put his arm around her waist and, with his other hand, bent her head in toward him so that it came to rest against his neck. They held each other in an embrace and sat for a while without speaking.

“But now I know what I am thinking about,” said Constance, pressing her lips against his beard.

“What, then, Conny?”

“About what we have spoken of so often: about how happy you have made me, about all our treasures, about everything we have lived through together, about the love you have brought to life in me by loving me, and especially about what you know—the thing that lies ahead.”

“My beloved, sweet one,” Lorck said, pressing her closer to him. “How happy you make me; how blissful your words are, and how sweet your caresses. And you, who were so afraid to take me—” he added a little later in a more tender voice.

“Not you any more than others; I felt reluctance or aversion, in general.”

“You wicked thing, who would have nothing to do with me. Do you remember how I had to struggle? And if the letter had not been—ugh, I dare not think of it.”

“It was a dreadful time,” said Constance. “What a creature I had become. That you truly had the courage to take me on was well done of you”—she clung to him.

“I loved you, Conny.”

“And in the beginning, when we were married—do you remember how foolish I was, utterly miserable with shyness?”

“Really, I have been rather persevering, Conny; you must admit that, for you did everything to discourage me. But, as I said, I loved you. I had never loved before I began to love you.”

“Is that really true, Nils? Tell me, is it true?”

“Yes, my dear, I know that now. If it had not been for you, I would never have learned to know love. And now, when we are expecting our treasure, I am supremely happy, Conny.”

“But you have nevertheless been in love with others—yes, and had relations with others?”

“It was nonsense and folly, Conny. Only you have made life come alive for me.”

“And it is the same for you too, Conny,” he continued a little later. “Your life begins only with me, does it not?”

She did not answer.

“For you love me; say that you love me.”

“You know I do, Nils,” she said softly.

“But say it all the same; it is so sweet to hear.”

A strange sensation came over her. She felt an urge to shake his arms off her and run away. It was as though something ghostly in the darkness were creeping up behind her, something she did not dare turn around to look at. It made her shudder. And then, at that same moment, she remembered the gentle pleasure that had stolen over her when Mejer, quite by chance that day, happened to place his arm on the back of the chair in which she was sitting. But now she wanted to get away from all this, and with a leap she plunged into the realm of thoughts of love and happiness in which she had lived for all these many months. She wrapped the memories of the sweet hours and all the enchanting little things that had passed between her and Lorck around herself like a shield. She would be happy, and that was that.

“I love you,” she said, “love, love you,” and her kisses and caresses were more passionate than ever before.

Lorck pressed her to his heart with a rapturous smile on his half-open lips. She hid her face in his soft, thick beard.

“But what is this?” he said with a sudden start. “I am becoming ill.” He grasped her hand and bent forward, groaning. Violent chills ran through him.

“You have caught cold from that ice,” said Constance. “Come, let us go up.”

With difficulty he rose and, supported by Constance’s arm, walked up through the garden and into the hotel; from time to time he stood still and moaned with pain.

When they had reached their rooms, Constance was alarmed by his pallor; a cold sweat lay on his brow, and he complained of unbearable nausea. She immediately sent for a doctor.

He was a somewhat elderly, short, stocky little Frenchman with masses of gray hair and beard. He told Constance that her husband had caught a severe cold, but that he hoped it would not become serious. Then he promised to send some medicine and to return the next morning.

XXV.

Lorck lay ill with gastric fever. Constance nursed him with tireless care. Most of the time he did not recognize her, but took her for someone else; he frequently called her Kristine.

The doctor obtained a deaconess who was to keep watch every other night, taking turns with Constance. He believed that three or four weeks would pass before they could even think about the journey home; otherwise there was no danger, provided only that they observed caution.
